stem: A 34-year-old man has had thick green penile discharge for 5 days and now a painful, swollen right testis; lifting the scrotum eases the pain. A Gram stain of the discharge is shown.

whyNot.D: **Motile flagellated protozoa** on a wet mount, not on Gram stain
whyNot.E: **Gram-negative rods** in men over 35 or with anal sex; urine infection rather than urethral pus

why: **Thick purulent discharge + Gram-negative diplococci inside neutrophils** = gonorrhea, here spread to the epididymis (pain eased by scrotal elevation).

whyNot.B: **Chains**, catalase negative, not clusters
whyNot.D: **Small Gram-negative coccobacilli**, stain pink

whyNot.C: **After gut or urinary procedures**, older patients, hospital setting
whyNot.D: **Lobar pneumonia or meningitis**; rarely infects valves
whyNot.E: **Prosthetic valves and catheters**; he has no prosthetic valve

whyNot.A: **Lancet-shaped pairs**, catalase negative
whyNot.B: **Chains**, catalase negative
whyNot.C: **Pairs and short chains**, catalase negative
whyNot.E: **Budding yeast** with pseudohyphae, not Gram-positive cocci in clusters

why: **Chronic sinusitis + bronchiectasis + dextrocardia** = Kartagener syndrome (primary ciliary dyskinesia). Cilia lacking dynein arms cannot clear mucus, so bacteria such as **S. aureus** settle in the lungs. **Clusters, catalase and coagulase positive** confirm it.

whyNot.D: **Curved Gram-negative rods**; undercooked poultry, fever, bloody stool after days
whyNot.E: **Gram-negative curved rods**; raw seafood

stem: An 8-month-old boy is brought in with 3 days of runny nose, cough and wheezing, and is found to have bronchiolitis. One of two blood culture bottles drawn in the emergency room grows Gram-positive cocci in clusters that are catalase positive, coagulase negative and novobiocin sensitive. He is afebrile and feeding better the next day.
oneliner: 8mo M + 3 d wheeze, runny nose (bronchiolitis) + 1 of 2 blood cultures positive: GPC clusters, catalase+, coagulase−, novobiocin sensitive → which organism?
ask: Which organism most likely grew in the culture?

whyNot.A: **Coagulase positive**, and would cause a sick child
whyNot.B: **Novobiocin resistant**; urinary infections in young women
whyNot.D: **Catalase negative**, lancet-shaped pairs
whyNot.E: **Catalase negative chains**, viridans group

why: **Cocci in clusters, catalase positive, coagulase negative, novobiocin sensitive** = S. epidermidis. Bronchiolitis is viral, and one positive bottle in a child who is improving is a **skin contaminant**.

bug.name: Staphylococcus epidermidis
bug.type: Gram-positive cocci in clusters; catalase positive
bug.lab: Coagulase negative; novobiocin sensitive
bug.virulence: Polysaccharide biofilm on plastic
bug.spread: Normal skin flora; enters on catheters, shunts, prosthetic valves and joints
bug.causes: Catheter and prosthetic-device infections; common blood culture contaminant

stem: A 24-year-old man is brought in with 1 day of headache, neck stiffness, confusion and a purpuric rash. His blood pressure is 70/40 mm Hg and platelets are falling with a prolonged prothrombin time. He has no ear pain and no recent travel. A Gram stain of his cerebrospinal fluid is shown.
oneliner: 24M + headache, stiff neck, confusion, purpura + shock with falling platelets, long PT + [CSF Gram stain] → which organism?
ask: Which organism is most likely responsible?

whyNot.B: **Gram-negative** (pink) kidney-bean diplococci
whyNot.C: **Small Gram-negative** coccobacilli; rare after Hib vaccination
whyNot.D: **Small Gram-positive rods**, at extremes of age or in pregnancy
whyNot.E: **Gram-negative rods**; newborn meningitis

why: **Purpuric rash with shock and DIC points to meningococcus, but the CSF shows Gram-positive lancet-shaped diplococci** = S. pneumoniae, which can also cause fulminant meningitis with DIC. The **capsule** is its main virulence factor.

ask: Which organism most likely caused this illness?

whyNot.A: Also alpha-hemolytic but **optochin resistant**; mouth flora, endocarditis
whyNot.B: **Beta-hemolytic**, in chains; throat and skin infection
whyNot.C: **Beta-hemolytic, hippurate positive**; newborn infections
whyNot.E: **Non-hemolytic**, grows in bile and 6.5% salt; hospital infections

why: **Abrupt lobar pneumonia with rust-colored sputum + Gram-positive diplococci that are alpha-hemolytic and optochin sensitive** = S. pneumoniae (also bile soluble).

stem: A 10-month-old boy has had 4 episodes of otitis media and 2 pneumonias since 6 months of age. He has no tonsils on examination. Serum IgG, IgA and IgM are all very low and flow cytometry finds almost no CD19-positive cells. Blood culture now grows alpha-hemolytic, optochin-sensitive Gram-positive diplococci.
oneliner: 10mo M + repeated otitis, 2 pneumonias after age 6 mo + no tonsils + all immunoglobulins low + no CD19 B cells + blood culture alpha-hemolytic, optochin sensitive diplococci → which organism?
ask: Which organism is isolated?

whyNot.A: **T-cell defects or AIDS**: bilateral interstitial pneumonia, whereas his defect is in B cells
whyNot.C: **T-cell defects**: thrush and mucocutaneous disease; a yeast, not a diplococcus
whyNot.D: **Neutropenia or CGD**: septate hyphae, not bacteria
whyNot.E: **Gut protozoan** causing chronic diarrhea; not seen in blood culture

why: **Boys with recurrent bacterial infections after maternal IgG fades, absent tonsils, no B cells and no immunoglobulins** = X-linked (Bruton) agammaglobulinemia from a BTK defect. Without antibody to opsonize capsules, **encapsulated bacteria such as S. pneumoniae** cause repeated infections.

stem: A 61-year-old man on hemodialysis through a subclavian catheter has had 3 days of low-grade fever. Two blood cultures grow Gram-positive cocci in pairs and short chains that are catalase negative and non-hemolytic.
oneliner: 61M + hemodialysis via subclavian catheter + 3 d low-grade fever + 2 blood cultures: GPC pairs and chains, catalase negative, non-hemolytic → which organism?
ask: Which organism is most likely responsible?

whyNot.B: **Clusters, catalase positive**
whyNot.C: **Clusters, catalase positive**, coagulase positive
whyNot.D: **Alpha-hemolytic** lancet-shaped pairs, optochin sensitive
whyNot.E: **Small Gram-positive rods**, beta-hemolytic, tumbling motility

why: **Catalase-negative, non-hemolytic Gram-positive cocci in pairs and chains from a catheter-related bacteremia** = Enterococcus faecalis, a gut commensal that grows in bile and 6.5% salt.

bug.name: Enterococcus faecalis
bug.type: Gram-positive cocci in pairs and short chains; catalase negative
bug.lab: Non-hemolytic; grows in bile and 6.5% NaCl (bile-esculin positive); PYR positive
bug.virulence: Intrinsic cephalosporin resistance; can acquire vancomycin resistance (vanA)
bug.spread: Gut flora; hospital and catheter exposure
bug.causes: Urinary tract infection, endocarditis after gut or urinary procedures, biliary and wound infection

stem: A 74-year-old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia has fever, flank pain and burning urination. Urine culture grows Gram-positive cocci in pairs and chains that are catalase negative, non-hemolytic and grow in 6.5% sodium chloride.

ask: Which organism most likely caused this pyelonephritis?

whyNot.B: **Clusters, catalase positive**
whyNot.C: **Beta-hemolytic chains**, bacitracin sensitive, **no growth in 6.5% salt**
whyNot.E: **Clusters, catalase positive**; sexually active young women

why: **Obstructed older man + Gram-positive urine isolate that is catalase negative, non-hemolytic and salt tolerant** = Enterococcus faecalis, the main Gram-positive urinary pathogen.

stem: A 47-year-old woman was started on ciprofloxacin 6 days ago for pyelonephritis. She now has 8 watery stools a day with lower abdominal cramps, a temperature of 38.2 °C and a white cell count of 18,000/mm3. The stool has no visible or occult blood. Sigmoidoscopy shows raised yellow-white plaques on the colonic mucosa.
oneliner: 47F + ciprofloxacin 6 d ago + 8 watery stools/day, cramps, low fever, WBC 18,000 + no blood + raised yellow-white colonic plaques → which organism?
ask: Which organism is most likely responsible?

whyNot.A: **Poultry or egg exposure**, fever and sometimes bloody stool; no antibiotic link
whyNot.C: **Bloody diarrhea without fever**, undercooked beef; here no blood
whyNot.D: **Weeks of greasy diarrhea** after drinking stream water; diagnosed by cysts or antigen
whyNot.E: **Food poisoning** 8 to 16 hours after reheated meat; not antibiotic related

why: **Watery diarrhea with leukocytosis and pseudomembranes after a quinolone** = C. difficile infection; the antibiotic wipes out competing flora. Diagnosis is by detecting **toxin A/B (or the toxin gene) in stool**; routine stool culture and ova-and-parasite exams do not help.

bug.name: Clostridioides difficile
bug.lab: Stool toxin A/B enzyme immunoassay or toxin-gene PCR; culture not used
bug.virulence: Toxin A (enterotoxin) and toxin B (cytotoxin) inactivate Rho GTPases; spores resist alcohol gel
bug.spread: Fecal-oral spores in hospitals; overgrowth after antibiotics (clindamycin, quinolones, cephalosporins)
bug.causes: Antibiotic-associated diarrhea, pseudomembranous colitis, toxic megacolon

stem: A 62-year-old man with diabetes and neuropathy has a foot ulcer that became black, foul-smelling and very painful over 2 days. The skin crackles when pressed and a plain film shows gas in the soft tissue. A Gram stain of the wound is shown.
oneliner: 62M + diabetic foot ulcer turning black, foul, painful over 2 d + crepitus, gas on film + [Gram stain] → which organism?
ask: Which organism is most likely responsible?

whyNot.A: **Clusters of cocci**, pus rather than gas
whyNot.B: **Pale Gram-negative** pleomorphic rods
whyNot.D: **Gram-negative rods** with blue-green pus, no gas
whyNot.E: **Terminal spores** and spastic paralysis, not gas and tissue death

why: **Painful, black, crepitant wound with gas in tissue + large Gram-positive rods** = gas gangrene from C. perfringens, driven by **alpha toxin**.

bug.name: Clostridium perfringens
bug.type: Large Gram-positive spore-forming anaerobic rod ('boxcar' shape)
bug.lab: Double zone of hemolysis on blood agar; lecithinase on egg-yolk agar (Nagler)
bug.virulence: Alpha toxin (lecithinase / phospholipase C); enterotoxin
bug.spread: Soil spores entering dead tissue; reheated meat dishes
bug.causes: Gas gangrene (myonecrosis); food poisoning with watery diarrhea 8-16 h after eating

stem: A 52-year-old woman with poor dentition has had a slowly enlarging, firm, painless swelling of her jaw for 2 months after a tooth extraction. Several draining sinus tracts discharge yellow granules, and a jaw film shows bone destruction. The organism grows only without oxygen and is not acid-fast. A Gram stain of a crushed granule is shown.
oneliner: 52F + poor teeth + 2 mo firm jaw swelling after extraction + draining sinuses with yellow granules + bone destruction + anaerobic, non-acid-fast + [Gram stain of granule] → which organism?
ask: Which organism most likely causes this infection?

whyNot.B: **Aerobic and weakly acid-fast**; soil exposure with lung or brain abscess in immunocompromised patients
whyNot.C: **Thin Gram-negative rods**; pharyngitis with jugular vein thrombosis
whyNot.D: **Short unbranched rods**; acne and prosthetic device infection
whyNot.E: **Gram-positive cocci in clusters** forming pus, not granules

why: **Dental trauma + slowly enlarging jaw mass with sinus tracts, yellow sulfur granules and branching Gram-positive anaerobic filaments** = cervicofacial actinomycosis ('lumpy jaw'), which responds to penicillin.

bug.name: Actinomyces israelii
bug.type: Branching filamentous Gram-positive anaerobe; not acid-fast
bug.lab: Yellow 'sulfur granules' in pus; strict anaerobe
bug.virulence: Normal mouth, gut and vaginal flora that invades after mucosal breaks
bug.spread: Not contagious; follows dental extraction, trauma, IUD use
bug.causes: Lumpy jaw (cervicofacial) with draining sinuses; thoracic, abdominal and pelvic (IUD) disease

stem: A 17-year-old sexually active girl has had 1 week of thin gray-yellow vaginal discharge with a fishy odor. She has no itching, dysuria or pelvic pain. Vaginal pH is 6.0 and adding 10% KOH to the discharge releases a fishy smell. A wet mount of the discharge is shown.
oneliner: 17F + sexually active + 1 wk thin gray-yellow fishy discharge + no itch or dysuria + pH 6.0 + positive KOH whiff test + [wet mount] → which organism?
ask: Which organism is most likely responsible?

whyNot.A: **Thick white curds with itching**; normal pH (4 to 4.5), pseudohyphae
whyNot.B: **Frothy green discharge, itching, motile pear-shaped protozoa** on wet mount
whyNot.C: **Intra-abdominal abscess** organism (Gram-negative anaerobic rod); not a cause of this picture
whyNot.E: **Painful vesicles or ulcers**; no discharge or fishy odor

why: **Thin gray discharge, pH above 4.5, positive whiff test and clue cells** = bacterial vaginosis, caused by overgrowth of Gardnerella and other anaerobes that replace lactobacilli.

bug.name: Gardnerella vaginalis
bug.lab: Clue cells on wet mount; vaginal pH above 4.5; positive whiff (KOH) test
bug.virulence: Biofilm replaces lactobacilli and raises vaginal pH
bug.spread: Linked to new or multiple sexual partners; not strictly an STI
bug.causes: Bacterial vaginosis (thin gray discharge, fishy odor); preterm birth risk

stem: A 22-year-old woman on day 3 of her period has had 3 days of fever and wandering joint pains, and now a swollen, painful right knee. A few tender pustules have appeared on her hands. A Gram stain of a cervical swab shows Gram-negative diplococci inside neutrophils. A photograph of her hand is shown.
oneliner: 22F + day 3 of period + fever, migrating joint pains, swollen knee + tender pustules on hands + cervical Gram stain: GN diplococci in neutrophils + [photo of hand] → which organism?
ask: Which organism is the most likely cause?

whyNot.A: **Obligate intracellular**: not seen on Gram stain
whyNot.C: **Gram-negative coccobacilli** causing a painful genital ulcer
whyNot.D: **Painless beefy-red genital ulcer** with Donovan bodies
whyNot.E: Causes **petechial or purpuric rash with meningitis and shock**, not pustules with migratory arthritis

why: **Menses + fever, migratory arthralgia, septic knee, acral pustules and Gram-negative diplococci in neutrophils** = disseminated gonococcal infection. It often appears in women **around menstruation**.

bug.name: Neisseria gonorrhoeae
bug.type: Gram-negative diplococcus (kidney-bean pairs), mostly inside neutrophils
bug.lab: Thayer-Martin agar; oxidase positive; ferments glucose only; NAAT
bug.virulence: Pili with antigenic variation (no lasting immunity, no vaccine), Opa proteins, IgA protease, LOS; no capsule
bug.spread: Sexual contact; birth canal
bug.causes: Urethritis, cervicitis, PID; disseminated infection with arthritis and pustules, especially in women during menses

stem: A 9-month-old boy whose parents declined all routine vaccines has had 1 day of fever, irritability, vomiting and a bulging fontanelle. The organism in his cerebrospinal fluid grows on chocolate agar but not on plain blood agar, and needs both hemin and NAD. A Gram stain of the CSF is shown.
oneliner: 9mo M + unvaccinated + fever, irritability, bulging fontanelle + CSF organism grows on chocolate not blood agar, needs hemin and NAD + [CSF Gram stain] → which organism?
ask: Which organism is most likely responsible?

whyNot.A: Grows on **blood agar**, kidney-bean diplococci
whyNot.B: Grows on **blood agar** with alpha-hemolysis; **Gram-positive** lancet-shaped diplococci
whyNot.C: Needs **Bordet-Gengou or Regan-Lowe agar**; respiratory, not meningitis
whyNot.E: **Gram-negative rods** growing easily on ordinary agar

why: **Unvaccinated infant with meningitis + Gram-negative coccobacilli that need X (hemin) and V (NAD) factors** = Hib. The **conjugate Hib vaccine** has made this rare.

bug.name: Haemophilus influenzae type b
bug.lab: Chocolate agar only (needs X = hemin and V = NAD); satellite growth around S. aureus
bug.virulence: Polyribitol phosphate capsule, IgA protease
bug.spread: Respiratory droplets; nasopharyngeal carriage
bug.causes: Meningitis, epiglottitis, pneumonia, otitis in unvaccinated children; prevented by conjugate Hib vaccine

stem: A 29-year-old man has had a very painful genital ulcer with a ragged, undermined edge and a gray base for 5 days, and a tender, enlarged right inguinal node that has started to drain pus. He had unprotected sex with a new partner 1 week before. A Gram stain of the ulcer exudate is shown.
oneliner: 29M + 5 d very painful genital ulcer, ragged undermined edge + tender draining inguinal node + new partner + [Gram stain of ulcer] → which organism?
ask: Which organism is most likely responsible?

whyNot.A: **Painless, clean-based, firm** chancre; too thin to see on Gram stain
whyNot.B: **Grouped small vesicles** with multinucleated giant cells on Tzanck smear
whyNot.C: **Painless beefy-red ulcer**; Donovan bodies seen on Giemsa stain
whyNot.D: **Obligate intracellular**; small painless ulcer, then matted nodes; no organisms on Gram stain

why: **Painful ragged soft ulcer + tender suppurative nodes + Gram-negative coccobacilli in chains** = chancroid. Any genital ulcer breaks the mucosal barrier, so chancroid also **raises the risk of acquiring HIV**; he should be tested.

bug.name: Haemophilus ducreyi
bug.type: Small Gram-negative coccobacillus in parallel chains ('school of fish')
bug.lab: Grows on chocolate agar with X factor (hemin) only
bug.virulence: Cytolethal distending toxin; invades broken genital skin
bug.spread: Sexual contact
bug.causes: Chancroid: painful ragged genital ulcer with tender suppurative nodes; raises HIV transmission and acquisition

stem: A 17-year-old boy has 2 days of belly pain that began around the navel and moved to the right lower abdomen. He now has fever, a rigid abdomen and a blood pressure of 88/50 mm Hg. CT shows a perforated appendix with free fluid. Gram stain of the peritoneal fluid shows Gram-negative rods, and aerobic culture grows pink colonies on MacConkey agar.

whyNot.D: **Non-lactose fermenter** (colorless on MacConkey); not a bowel-flora peritonitis organism
whyNot.E: **Non-lactose fermenter**, swarms on agar; mainly urinary

whyNot.C: **Non-lactose fermenter**; after catheters or hospital stay
whyNot.E: **No cell wall**, not seen on Gram stain or routine culture

why: **Acute prostatitis (tender, boggy prostate) in a man over 35 with lactose-fermenting Gram-negative rods** = E. coli, the commonest cause. In young men chlamydia and gonorrhea take over.

whyNot.D: **Gram-positive lancet diplococci**
whyNot.E: Tiny **coccobacilli** seen in unvaccinated infants over 2 months, not newborns

why: **Neonatal meningitis with Gram-negative rods in CSF** = E. coli. Strains with the **K1 capsule** resist phagocytosis and complement, and cross the blood-brain barrier.

bug.name: Escherichia coli (K1 strains)
bug.lab: Pink on MacConkey; indole positive; Gram-negative rods in CSF
bug.virulence: K1 capsule (sialic acid) resists phagocytosis and complement
bug.spread: Vaginal or gut flora acquired at birth

whyNot.D: **Non-lactose fermenter**, oxidase positive; catheters and hospitalization
whyNot.E: **Diplococci** that do not grow on MacConkey; discharge expected

why: **Uncomplicated cystitis with nitrite-positive urine and lactose-fermenting, indole-positive rods** = E. coli, the cause of most cystitis. It reduces nitrate to nitrite.

stem: A 29-year-old man develops cramps and profuse watery diarrhea 2 days after returning from a trip to Mexico. He has no fever and no blood in the stool. Stool microscopy shows no white cells.
oneliner: 29M + back from Mexico + watery diarrhea, cramps + no fever, no blood, no fecal leukocytes → which organism?
ask: Which organism is the most likely cause?

whyNot.A: **Fever, bloody mucoid stool** with fecal neutrophils
whyNot.B: **Poultry exposure**, often bloody, comma or gull-wing rods
whyNot.C: **Bloody diarrhea** over weeks, liver abscess
whyNot.E: **Prolonged fever, rose spots**, constipation then diarrhea

why: **Watery diarrhea after travel with no fever, blood or fecal white cells** = a toxin-mediated, non-invasive process. ETEC sticks with **fimbriae** and releases **heat-labile toxin (cAMP up, like cholera)** and heat-stable toxin (cGMP up).

bug.name: Enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (ETEC)
bug.lab: Pink on MacConkey; diagnosed clinically
bug.virulence: Colonization-factor fimbriae; heat-labile toxin (raises cAMP like cholera toxin) and heat-stable toxin (raises cGMP)
bug.spread: Fecal-oral; contaminated food and water
bug.causes: Traveler's watery diarrhea, no blood or fever

stem: A 4-year-old girl had bloody diarrhea after a family barbecue where burgers were undercooked. Five days later she is pale and her urine output has dropped. Blood pressure is 125/85 mm Hg. Hemoglobin is 7.8 g/dL, platelets 48,000/mm3 and creatinine 2.4 mg/dL. A peripheral blood smear is shown.
oneliner: 4F + bloody diarrhea after undercooked burgers, then pallor, oliguria, hypertension + anemia, low platelets, high creatinine + [smear] → which organism?
ask: Which organism is the most likely cause of her initial illness?

whyNot.A: Bloody diarrhea from **poultry**, but triggers **Guillain-Barre**, not HUS
whyNot.B: **Eggs and poultry**; fever, and no Shiga toxin
whyNot.C: **Non-bloody** watery diarrhea in infants
whyNot.D: **Pork, raw milk**; pseudoappendicitis

why: **Bloody diarrhea from undercooked beef, then anemia, thrombocytopenia and kidney injury with schistocytes** = hemolytic uremic syndrome from Shiga toxin-producing E. coli. The toxin **cleaves 28S rRNA of the 60S ribosome**, killing endothelial cells and forming microthrombi.

bug.name: Escherichia coli O157:H7 (EHEC)
bug.lab: Does not ferment sorbitol (colorless on sorbitol-MacConkey)
bug.virulence: Shiga toxin: cleaves 28S rRNA of the 60S ribosome, killing gut and endothelial cells
bug.spread: Undercooked ground beef, unpasteurized juice or milk; low infectious dose
bug.causes: Bloody diarrhea without fever; hemolytic uremic syndrome

stem: A 34-year-old kindergarten teacher has 2 days of fever, cramps and frequent small stools containing blood and mucus, with a constant urge to defecate. Several children in her class had the same illness last week. A methylene blue stain of her stool is shown.
oneliner: 34F + kindergarten teacher, outbreak in class + fever, cramps, small bloody mucoid stools, tenesmus + [stool methylene blue] → which organism?
ask: Which organism is most likely responsible?

whyNot.B: **Stepwise high fever, rose spots**, constipation before diarrhea
whyNot.C: Follows **recent antibiotics**; pseudomembranes
whyNot.D: **Raw poultry** exposure; curved rods; not a classroom outbreak
whyNot.E: **Painless rice-water** stools, no blood

why: **Bloody mucoid stools with tenesmus and fecal neutrophils, spreading among young children** = Shigella. Only **10 to 100 organisms** cause disease, so person-to-person spread is easy; it invades M cells and releases **Shiga toxin**.

bug.name: Shigella species
bug.lab: Non-lactose fermenter; H2S negative; fecal neutrophils
bug.virulence: Invades M cells and spreads by actin rockets; Shiga toxin cleaves the 60S ribosome
bug.spread: Fecal-oral; very low infectious dose (10 to 100 organisms)
bug.causes: Bloody mucoid diarrhea with tenesmus (dysentery)

stem: A 7-year-old boy on a dairy farm has fever, diarrhea and right lower quadrant pain for 4 days after drinking raw milk. Appendix imaging is normal. A stool sample kept in a refrigerator at 4 C for 2 weeks grows a non-lactose-fermenting Gram-negative coccobacillus.
oneliner: 7M + dairy farm, raw milk + fever, diarrhea, RLQ pain, normal appendix + stool culture grows after cold enrichment at 4 C → which organism?
ask: Which organism is the most likely cause?

whyNot.A: Grows best at **42 C**, curved rods, poultry source
whyNot.B: **Prolonged fever, rose spots**; does not need cold enrichment
whyNot.C: **Painless watery** stools; no abdominal tenderness
whyNot.D: **Lactose fermenter**; no cold growth

why: **Raw milk or pork + fever, diarrhea and right lower quadrant pain with a normal appendix** (mesenteric adenitis, pseudoappendicitis) and **growth at 4 C** = Y. enterocolitica.

bug.name: Yersinia enterocolitica
bug.lab: Grows at 4 C (cold enrichment); non-lactose fermenter
bug.virulence: Invasin, enterotoxin; yersiniabactin siderophore
bug.spread: Pork, unpasteurized milk; contaminated stored blood
bug.causes: Enterocolitis, mesenteric adenitis mimicking appendicitis

stem: A 28-year-old man develops explosive watery diarrhea and cramps 24 hours after eating raw oysters at a party. He has no fever and no blood in the stool, and he recovers over 2 days. Stool grows curved Gram-negative rods that form green colonies on TCBS agar.
oneliner: 28M + raw oysters 24 h earlier + watery diarrhea, cramps, no fever or blood + curved GNR, green colonies on TCBS → which organism?
ask: Which organism is the most likely cause?

whyNot.A: **Gram-positive spore-forming rod** from reheated rice
whyNot.C: **Poultry**, 2 to 5 day incubation, often bloody
whyNot.D: **Gram-positive**, undercooked meat, no TCBS growth
whyNot.E: **Gram-positive cocci**, preformed toxin, vomiting within 1 to 6 hours

why: **Raw oysters + watery diarrhea + green colonies of curved Gram-negative rods on TCBS** = V. parahaemolyticus (halophilic). V. cholerae gives **yellow** colonies and V. vulnificus causes wound infection and sepsis in liver disease.

bug.name: Vibrio parahaemolyticus
bug.lab: Green colonies on TCBS agar; oxidase positive; needs salt to grow
bug.virulence: Thermostable direct hemolysin (Kanagawa); enterotoxin
bug.spread: Raw or undercooked seafood, especially oysters
bug.causes: Self-limited watery gastroenteritis; wound infection

stem: A 19-year-old woman has an itchy rash of red bumps and small pustules on her trunk and thighs that began 2 days after using a hotel hot tub. She has no fever. A photograph of her trunk is shown.
oneliner: 19F + itchy red follicular pustules on trunk and thighs 2 d after hot tub + no fever + [photo] → which organism?
ask: Which organism is most likely responsible?

whyNot.A: Common folliculitis in hairy areas, **no water link**; Gram-positive cocci
whyNot.B: **Cellulitis or impetigo** with spreading redness or honey crusts
whyNot.D: **Greasy upper back and chest** follicular papules, not tied to water
whyNot.E: **Moist skin folds** with satellite pustules

why: **Pustular rash on the body areas covered by swimwear after hot tub or pool use** = hot tub folliculitis. Pseudomonas thrives in warm, poorly chlorinated water and resolves without treatment.

bug.name: Pseudomonas aeruginosa
bug.lab: Oxidase positive; non-lactose fermenter; blue-green pigment (pyocyanin); grape-like odor
bug.virulence: Exotoxin A (blocks EF-2), pyocyanin, biofilm, endotoxin
bug.spread: Water and moist environments, hospital equipment, hot tubs
bug.causes: Hot tub folliculitis, burn and wound infection, ventilator pneumonia, otitis externa, UTI

stem: A 28-year-old man has fever and a very tender, swollen lump in the right groin 4 days after a camping trip in Arizona where he moved a dead ground squirrel. A Giemsa stain of fluid aspirated from the lump is shown.
oneliner: 28M + Arizona camping, dead ground squirrel + fever + very tender groin node (bubo) + [aspirate stain] → which organism?
ask: Which organism is most likely responsible?

whyNot.B: **Rabbits or ticks**, ulcer at the bite site, then nodes
whyNot.C: **Cat scratch**, small papule, mildly tender node
whyNot.D: **Unpasteurized dairy**, undulant fever, no bubo
whyNot.E: **Sexually acquired** painful genital ulcer with tender groin node

why: **Fever + tender bubo after rodent and flea exposure in the US Southwest** = bubonic plague. The aspirate shows **bipolar-staining ('safety pin') coccobacilli**.

bug.name: Yersinia pestis
bug.type: Gram-negative coccobacillus with bipolar ("safety pin") staining
bug.lab: Giemsa or Wright stain shows bipolar staining; grows slowly at 28 C
bug.virulence: Capsular F1 antigen, V and W antigens, Yops, coagulase and plasminogen activator
bug.spread: Flea bite (Xenopsylla) from rodents, e.g. prairie dogs and ground squirrels in the US southwest
bug.causes: Bubonic plague (buboes), pneumonic plague, septicemic plague

stem: A 9-year-old girl has a small red papule on the back of her hand and, 3 weeks later, a tender swollen right armpit lymph node and a temperature of 38.1 C. She has a new pet kitten. A silver stain of the lymph node is shown.
oneliner: 9F + hand papule then tender axillary node + new kitten + low fever + [silver stain of node] → which organism?

whyNot.A: **Rabbit or tick** exposure; ulcer at the site
whyNot.C: **Cat bite** with rapid cellulitis within 24 hours
whyNot.D: **Unpasteurized dairy**, undulant fever
whyNot.E: **Rat bite** fever with rash and arthritis

why: **Kitten + papule at a scratch site + tender regional node weeks later** = cat-scratch disease. The **Warthin-Starry silver stain** shows small pleomorphic bacilli; cat fleas spread the organism between cats.

bug.name: Bartonella henselae
bug.lab: Warthin-Starry silver stain; serology (IFA) or PCR; hard to culture
bug.virulence: Adhesins; stimulates new vessel growth (angiomatosis)
bug.spread: Cat scratch or bite; cat fleas carry it between cats
bug.causes: Cat-scratch disease, bacillary angiomatosis (HIV), endocarditis

stem: A 24-year-old man has a ruptured appendix and a right lower quadrant abscess drained at surgery. The pus smells foul and its Gram stain shows many mixed Gram-negative rods, yet routine aerobic culture grows only enterococci.
oneliner: 24M + ruptured appendix, abscess + foul pus + mixed Gram-negative rods but aerobic culture grows only enterococci → which missed organism?
ask: Which organism most likely accounts for the abscess but failed to grow?

whyNot.A: **Grows readily in aerobic culture**, so would have been recovered
whyNot.B: **Aerobic**, would grow on routine plates
whyNot.C: **Lung pathogen** needing special media; not a bowel organism
whyNot.D: **Respiratory diplococcus**

why: **Foul pus from a bowel source, Gram-negative rods on smear, and no aerobic growth** = anaerobic bowel flora. Bacteroides fragilis is the commonest; its **capsule promotes abscess formation**. Treat with metronidazole.

bug.lab: Needs anaerobic culture; bile resistant; does not grow in routine aerobic cultures
bug.virulence: Polysaccharide capsule (abscess formation), beta-lactamase, endotoxin that is weak
bug.spread: Colonic flora spilling after bowel rupture or surgery
bug.causes: Intra-abdominal and pelvic abscess, peritonitis; treated with metronidazole

stem: A 2-month-old boy, born at term with no problems, has had persistent bloody nasal discharge and noisy breathing. He has cracked skin around his mouth and anus and an enlarged liver and spleen. His mother had no prenatal care.

whyNot.B: **Vesicles, encephalitis** in the first weeks
whyNot.C: **Microcephaly, periventricular calcifications**, hearing loss
whyNot.D: **Recurrent infections and poor growth** months later; no rhinitis or fissures

whyNot.C: Rare in newborns; **purulent** with respiratory illness
whyNot.D: Retinitis in congenital infection; **not a sticky conjunctivitis**

whyNot.D: Causes **vaginosis in women**, not urethritis
whyNot.E: **Warts**, no urethritis or pyuria

whyNot.E: **Swollen parotid glands**, not mouth ulcers or hand lesions

why: **Fever + painful oral ulcers + vesicles on palms (and soles) in a daycare child** = hand-foot-and-mouth disease from coxsackievirus A, a picornavirus spread by the fecal-oral and respiratory routes.

bug.name: Coxsackievirus A
bug.lab: Throat, stool or vesicle PCR or culture; acid-stable
bug.virulence: Capsid survives stomach acid; replicates in oropharynx and gut lymphoid tissue
bug.spread: Fecal-oral and respiratory droplets; daycare outbreaks
bug.causes: Hand-foot-and-mouth disease, herpangina, aseptic meningitis

image.prompt: Palm and fingers of a young child's hand with several small oval grey-white vesicles surrounded by thin red halos; a few similar lesions on the sides of the fingers; no other rash

stem: A 16-year-old boy has had 3 days of sharp central chest pain that is worse when lying flat and eases when he leans forward. It began 5 days after a febrile illness with sore throat and diarrhea that settled by itself. A scratchy sound is heard over the left sternal edge, and his temperature is 37.8 C. Blood cultures are negative.
oneliner: 16M + sharp chest pain worse supine, better leaning forward + friction rub after a febrile illness + negative blood cultures → which organism?
ask: Which organism is the most likely cause?

whyNot.A: **Purulent pericarditis**: high fever, toxic appearance and **positive blood cultures**
whyNot.B: **Weeks of night sweats and weight loss**, effusion that may become constrictive
whyNot.C: **Parotid swelling** and orchitis; not a typical cause of pericarditis
whyNot.E: **Rheumatic carditis** weeks after pharyngitis, with migratory arthritis

why: **Postural pleuritic chest pain + friction rub after a self-limited febrile illness, negative cultures** = viral pericarditis, most often **coxsackievirus B**. The same virus causes pleurodynia (devil's grip).

bug.name: Coxsackievirus B
bug.lab: PCR of throat, stool, pericardial fluid or biopsy
bug.virulence: Replicates in heart and pleura; capsid is acid-stable
bug.spread: Fecal-oral and respiratory droplets
bug.causes: Myocarditis, pericarditis, pleurodynia (devil's grip), aseptic meningitis

stem: A 29-year-old woman has 3 days of breathlessness, needing three pillows to sleep, and ankle swelling, starting a week after a flu-like illness. Echocardiography shows a dilated, poorly contracting left ventricle with normal coronary arteries. Endomyocardial biopsy shows lymphocytes among necrotic myocytes, and PCR identifies a non-enveloped, single-stranded positive-sense RNA virus.
oneliner: 29F + dyspnea, orthopnea, edema 1 wk after flu-like illness + dilated poorly contracting LV, clean coronaries + biopsy PCR: non-enveloped ssRNA(+) virus → which organism?
ask: Which organism is most likely responsible?

whyNot.B: Also causes myocarditis, but is a **non-enveloped double-stranded DNA** virus
whyNot.C: **Enveloped DNA virus**; typically mucocutaneous or encephalitic disease
whyNot.D: **Enveloped, segmented negative-sense RNA** virus
whyNot.E: **Non-enveloped single-stranded DNA** virus; erythema infectiosum and aplastic crisis

why: **Dilated cardiomyopathy picture after a viral prodrome + lymphocytic infiltrate with myocyte necrosis** = myocarditis. A **non-enveloped ssRNA(+) picornavirus** points to **coxsackievirus B**, the commonest cause.

bug.name: Coxsackievirus B
bug.lab: PCR of throat, stool, pericardial fluid or biopsy
bug.virulence: Replicates in heart and pleura; capsid is acid-stable
bug.spread: Fecal-oral and respiratory droplets
bug.causes: Myocarditis, pericarditis, pleurodynia (devil's grip), aseptic meningitis

stem: A 9-year-old boy in August has 2 days of fever, headache, light sensitivity and a stiff neck. Two classmates have a similar illness. He is fully vaccinated. Lumbar puncture shows 220 white cells/uL (85% lymphocytes), mildly raised protein and normal glucose; Gram stain shows no organisms.
oneliner: 9M + August + fever, headache, photophobia, neck stiffness + classmates ill + CSF 220 cells (85% lymphocytes), normal glucose → which organism?
ask: Which organism is most likely responsible?

whyNot.A: Usually **adults with genital herpes**; recurrent (Mollaret) episodes
whyNot.B: **Neutrophils, low glucose**, organisms on Gram stain, very sick child
whyNot.C: **Neutrophilic CSF with low glucose**, petechial rash, rapid collapse
whyNot.D: Also lymphocytic CSF, but he is **fully vaccinated** and has no parotid swelling

why: **Summer outbreak + lymphocytic CSF with normal glucose and a negative Gram stain** = viral (aseptic) meningitis. **Enteroviruses** (coxsackie, echo) are by far the most common cause.

bug.name: Enterovirus (coxsackie, echovirus)
bug.lab: CSF: lymphocytes, normal glucose, mildly raised protein; CSF RT-PCR
bug.virulence: Acid-stable capsid; spreads to meninges by viremia
bug.spread: Fecal-oral; summer and autumn outbreaks
bug.causes: Most common cause of viral (aseptic) meningitis

stem: A 3-year-old girl who recently arrived from rural Nigeria with her family has never been vaccinated. After 3 days of fever and back pain, she cannot bear weight on her left leg. The left leg is floppy with absent reflexes and visible muscle twitching; sensation is normal. A cousin in the village has a similar illness. CSF shows mild lymphocytosis.
oneliner: 3F + from rural Nigeria, unvaccinated + fever, back pain then floppy left leg, no reflexes, twitching, normal sensation + cousin ill → which organism?
ask: Which organism is the most likely cause?

whyNot.A: Causes **hand-foot-and-mouth disease**; paralysis is not its classic picture
whyNot.B: **Culex mosquito bites** in elderly adults with encephalitis; not a child from a village outbreak
whyNot.D: Needs a **bite from a rabid animal**, then agitation and hydrophobia
whyNot.E: **Fever with temporal lobe encephalitis**, seizures and behavior change, not flaccid paralysis

why: **Unvaccinated child + fever then asymmetric flaccid paralysis with fasciculations and normal sensation** = destruction of anterior horn cells (lower motor neuron) by poliovirus, spread fecal-orally.

bug.name: Poliovirus (three serotypes)
bug.lab: Virus isolated from stool or throat; CSF mild lymphocytosis
bug.virulence: Replicates in gut lymphoid tissue, viremia, then infects anterior horn motor neurons
bug.spread: Fecal-oral
bug.causes: Mostly asymptomatic; aseptic meningitis; asymmetric flaccid paralysis; post-polio syndrome

stem: A 3-year-old boy with AIDS (CD4 count 40/uL) has had 2 weeks of cough, fever and increasing breathlessness with low oxygen saturation. His sister recently had a fever and a red blotchy rash, but he has no rash. A lung biopsy is shown.
oneliner: 3M + AIDS + cough, fever, hypoxia + sibling had maculopapular rash + no rash himself + [lung biopsy] → which organism?
ask: Which organism is most likely responsible?

whyNot.A: Abrupt **fever with myalgia in winter**; no giant cells
whyNot.B: **Bronchiolitis with wheeze in infants**; no sibling with a rash
whyNot.D: **Owl's-eye** nuclear inclusions in pneumonitis; no rash contact
whyNot.E: **Smudge cells** and conjunctivitis or hemorrhagic cystitis

why: **AIDS + exposure to a rash illness + pneumonia without a rash + multinucleated giant cells with inclusions** = measles giant cell (Warthin-Finkeldey) pneumonia. Without T cells he makes **no rash**, because the rash is a T-cell reaction.

bug.name: Measles virus
bug.type: Enveloped, non-segmented single-stranded negative-sense RNA paramyxovirus
bug.lab: Koplik spots; multinucleated giant cells; IgM or RT-PCR
bug.virulence: Hemagglutinin binds CD150 (SLAM); fusion protein makes syncytia; transient immune suppression
bug.spread: Airborne; extremely contagious
bug.causes: Measles (cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, rash); giant cell pneumonia; otitis media; SSPE

image.prompt: H&E lung biopsy: alveolar spaces lined by large multinucleated syncytial giant cells containing many nuclei with pink (eosinophilic) intranuclear and cytoplasmic inclusion bodies, surrounded by mild interstitial inflammation

stem: A 19-year-old university student whose parents declined childhood vaccines has had 3 days of fever and malaise, then painful swelling in front of both ears. Chewing sour food makes the pain worse. A photograph of his face is shown. Serum amylase is raised.
oneliner: 19M + unvaccinated + fever, malaise, then painful bilateral swelling in front of ears, pain on chewing sour food, high amylase + [photo] → which organism?
ask: Which organism is most likely responsible?

whyNot.A: **Suppurative parotitis**: usually one-sided, pus from the duct, dehydrated or elderly patient
whyNot.B: **Exudative pharyngitis, posterior neck nodes**, splenomegaly
whyNot.C: **Mononucleosis-like illness**, usually without parotid swelling
whyNot.E: **Sore throat with fever**, strep tonsillitis; not bilateral parotid swelling

why: **Unvaccinated young adult + bilateral parotid swelling + high amylase** = mumps, a paramyxovirus spread by respiratory droplets and saliva.

bug.name: Mumps virus
bug.lab: Raised serum amylase; IgM or PCR
bug.virulence: Hemagglutinin-neuraminidase and fusion proteins; tropism for glands and meninges
bug.spread: Respiratory droplets and saliva
bug.causes: Parotitis, orchitis, aseptic meningitis, pancreatitis, sensorineural deafness

image.prompt: Frontal view of a young man's face with visible symmetric swelling of both cheeks in front of and below the ears, earlobes pushed outward, skin of normal color

stem: A 31-year-old woman developed sudden vomiting, watery diarrhea and cramps about 36 hours after a wedding reception where roughly 40 guests became ill. Her temperature is 37.8 C; stool has no blood or white cells and routine cultures are negative. Her toddler became ill two days later. Everyone recovered within 48 hours.
oneliner: 31F + vomiting, watery diarrhea 36 h after wedding + many guests ill + no blood or WBC in stool + cultures negative + toddler ill 2 d later → which organism?
ask: Which organism is most likely responsible?

whyNot.A: **Infants and young children**, winter; adult outbreaks after a wedding are not typical
whyNot.C: **Preformed toxin**, illness within 1 to 6 hours, no secondary cases
whyNot.D: **Bloody diarrhea with fever** and white cells in stool
whyNot.E: **Weeks** of foul greasy diarrhea after drinking stream water

why: **Explosive vomiting and watery diarrhea 1 to 2 days after a shared event, no blood or leukocytes, negative cultures, household spread** = norovirus, a non-enveloped calicivirus with a very low infectious dose.

bug.name: Norovirus
bug.lab: Stool RT-PCR; routine bacterial cultures negative
bug.virulence: Very low infectious dose; survives alcohol hand rubs and many disinfectants
bug.spread: Fecal-oral; vomitus aerosols; food handlers; cruise ships
bug.causes: Self-limited vomiting and watery diarrhea lasting 1 to 3 days

stem: A 2-day-old girl has a small head, cloudy white pupils in both eyes and a continuous machine-like murmur. Her mother emigrated recently, has never been immunized, and had a mild rash with tender swollen nodes behind both ears during week 8 of pregnancy.
oneliner: 2-day-old F + microcephaly, bilateral cataracts, continuous murmur + mother never immunized, week-8 rash with postauricular nodes → which organism?
ask: Which organism is most likely responsible?

whyNot.A: **Periventricular calcifications** and sensorineural deafness; usually no cataracts or PDA
whyNot.B: **Skin vesicles, encephalitis** at birth after vaginal delivery
whyNot.C: **Limb hypoplasia and skin scars** after maternal chickenpox
whyNot.E: **Hydrocephalus with diffuse calcifications** and chorioretinitis; maternal cat or raw meat exposure

why: **First-trimester maternal rash with postauricular nodes + cataracts, patent ductus murmur, small head** = congenital rubella. A live MMR vaccine before pregnancy prevents it.

bug.name: Rubella virus
bug.lab: IgM anti-rubella; IgG for immunity screening
bug.virulence: Crosses the placenta, worst in first trimester; live MMR vaccine prevents it
bug.spread: Respiratory droplets; transplacental
bug.causes: Mild rash with postauricular nodes; congenital rubella: PDA, cataracts, deafness, microcephaly

stem: A 72-year-old gardener in late August has had 4 days of fever and headache, then confusion and sudden weakness of the right arm. He has many mosquito bites and dead crows were found in his yard. CSF shows lymphocytes with normal glucose and is positive for IgM against a flavivirus.
oneliner: 72M + late August + fever, headache, confusion, right arm weakness + mosquito bites, dead crows + CSF lymphocytes, normal glucose, flavivirus IgM → which organism?
ask: Which organism is most likely responsible?

whyNot.B: **Aedes mosquito**, tropical travel, break-bone pain, rash and low platelets
whyNot.C: **Africa or South America**, jaundice and bleeding; prevented by a live vaccine
whyNot.D: **Unvaccinated child** after fecal-oral spread; no mosquito or bird link
whyNot.E: **Temporal lobe encephalitis** with hemorrhagic CSF and seizures

why: **Late summer + Culex bites + dead birds + encephalitis with flaccid weakness in an older adult** = West Nile virus, a flavivirus with a bird reservoir; humans are dead-end hosts.

bug.name: West Nile virus
bug.lab: IgM in serum or CSF; RT-PCR
bug.virulence: Neuroinvasive; can destroy anterior horn cells
bug.spread: Culex mosquito; birds are the reservoir; humans are dead-end hosts
bug.causes: Fever; encephalitis and meningitis, especially in the elderly; acute flaccid paralysis

stem: A 58-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes has had 5 days of intense vulvar itching, burning with intercourse, and a thick white odorless discharge. She has one long-term partner. The vulva is red and swollen; vaginal pH is 4.2. A potassium hydroxide wet mount of the discharge is shown.
oneliner: 58F + type 2 diabetes + itching, dyspareunia, thick white odorless discharge, red swollen vulva, pH 4.2 + [KOH mount] → which organism?
ask: Which organism is most likely responsible?

whyNot.A: **Frothy green-yellow malodorous discharge, pH above 4.5**, motile flagellates on wet mount
whyNot.B: **Thin gray fishy discharge**, pH above 4.5, no itching, clue cells
whyNot.C: Usually **silent cervicitis** with mucopurulent discharge; no organisms on a wet mount
whyNot.E: **Painful vesicles and ulcers**, not thick white discharge

why: **Diabetes + pruritus + thick white odorless discharge + normal pH (4.2) + yeast and pseudohyphae on KOH** = Candida vulvovaginitis. High glucose in secretions feeds the yeast; the normal pH separates it from trichomonas and bacterial vaginosis.

bug.name: Candida albicans
bug.lab: Germ tube positive at 37 C; KOH prep shows yeast and pseudohyphae; cream colonies on Sabouraud agar
bug.virulence: Adhesins, biofilm on catheters, yeast-to-hypha switch, secreted proteases
bug.spread: Normal flora of mouth, gut and vagina; overgrowth with antibiotics or hyperglycemia; central lines
bug.causes: Thrush, vulvovaginitis, esophagitis, candidemia, endocarditis

image.prompt: KOH wet mount microscopy: many oval budding yeast cells with several long branching pseudohyphae (chains of elongated cells), epithelial cell debris dissolved, clear background

stem: A 61-year-old woman with Crohn disease has been receiving total parenteral nutrition through a central venous catheter for 3 weeks. She has persistent fever for 6 days despite broad-spectrum antibiotics. Blood cultures grow creamy white colonies on blood agar; a Gram stain of the growth is shown.
oneliner: 61F + Crohn disease on TPN via central line 3 wk + fever 6 d despite broad-spectrum antibiotics + creamy colonies, [Gram stain] → which organism?
ask: Which organism is most likely responsible?

whyNot.B: **Encapsulated yeast without pseudohyphae**, causes meningitis in AIDS; India ink positive
whyNot.C: **Septate hyphae branching at acute angles**, lung disease; not budding yeast
whyNot.D: **Broad non-septate hyphae**, diabetic ketoacidosis, rhinocerebral disease
whyNot.E: **Bacterial cocci in clusters**, not oval budding forms

why: **Central line + parenteral nutrition + fever unresponsive to antibiotics + budding yeast with pseudohyphae** = candidemia. Candida forms **biofilm on catheters**; the lipid-rich TPN feeds it. Remove the line and treat with an echinocandin.

bug.name: Candida albicans
bug.lab: Germ tube positive at 37 C; KOH prep shows yeast and pseudohyphae; cream colonies on Sabouraud agar
bug.virulence: Adhesins, biofilm on catheters, yeast-to-hypha switch, secreted proteases
bug.spread: Normal flora of mouth, gut and vagina; overgrowth with antibiotics or hyperglycemia; central lines
bug.causes: Thrush, vulvovaginitis, esophagitis, candidemia, endocarditis

image.prompt: Gram stain of colony growth: numerous oval purple (Gram-positive) budding yeast cells, 4 to 6 micrometres, with some elongated pseudohyphae, no bacteria

stem: A 41-year-old man with AIDS who stopped his antiretroviral drugs dies after 3 weeks of headache, confusion and low-grade fever. At autopsy the meninges are thickened and gelatinous. A mucicarmine-stained section of the meninges is shown.
oneliner: 41M + AIDS off treatment + 3 wk headache, confusion, low fever + gelatinous meninges + [mucicarmine-stained meningeal section] → which organism?
ask: Which organism most likely caused his death?

whyNot.B: **Yeast with pseudohyphae**: thrush or esophagitis, rarely meningitis, and not capsule-stained red
whyNot.C: **Ring-enhancing brain masses** with focal deficits, not diffuse meningitis
whyNot.D: **Acid-fast bacilli** with diarrhea, fever and wasting; not a meningeal yeast
whyNot.E: **Pneumonia** with cough and low oxygen; cysts in lung, not meninges

why: **AIDS + subacute meningitis + yeast whose capsule stains red with mucicarmine in the meninges** = cryptococcal meningitis. Mucicarmine stains the **polysaccharide capsule**.

bug.name: Cryptococcus neoformans
bug.lab: India ink: halo around yeast; mucicarmine stains capsule red; urease positive; capsular antigen test
bug.virulence: Polysaccharide capsule blocks phagocytosis; melanin from phenol oxidase
bug.spread: Inhaled from soil and pigeon droppings; not person to person
bug.causes: Meningitis (AIDS, CD4 <100), pneumonia

image.prompt: Meningeal section stained with mucicarmine: many round yeast cells of varying size in the subarachnoid space, capsules stained deep pink-red, some narrow-based buds, a few inflammatory cells, soap-bubble appearance

stem: A 29-year-old man, a farm worker, who moved from the San Joaquin Valley of central California three weeks ago has fever, dry cough, joint pains and tender red nodules on his shins. A lactophenol blue preparation of a mold grown from his sputum at room temperature is shown.
oneliner: 29M + recently left central California farmland + fever, dry cough, joint pain, tender shin nodules + [mold culture preparation] → which organism?
ask: Which organism is most likely responsible?

whyNot.A: **Ohio and Mississippi river valleys**, bat and bird droppings; not central California
whyNot.B: **Great Lakes and southeastern states**; broad-based budding yeast with skin and bone lesions
whyNot.C: **Opportunistic mold** in neutropenia, asthma or old lung cavities; not a healthy farm worker with erythema nodosum
whyNot.D: **Latin America only**; ship-wheel budding yeast with mouth and skin lesions; not central California

why: **Central California + pneumonia with erythema nodosum + mold with barrel-shaped arthroconidia** = Coccidioides (San Joaquin Valley fever). Inhaled arthroconidia turn into **spherules** at body temperature.

bug.name: Coccidioides immitis
bug.type: Dimorphic fungus (mold in soil, spherules in tissue)
bug.lab: 25°C: mold with arthroconidia; tissue: spherules packed with endospores
bug.virulence: Inhaled arthroconidia; spherules resist phagocytosis
bug.spread: Inhaled dust, US Southwest and central California; not person to person
bug.causes: Valley fever pneumonia, erythema nodosum, meningitis, dissemination (pregnancy, immunosuppression)

image.prompt: Lactophenol blue preparation of a mold: septate hyphae breaking into chains of barrel-shaped rectangular arthroconidia separated by empty cells

stem: A 34-year-old man returns from a work trip to India with 4 days of spiking fevers, shaking chills and confusion. He is hypotensive, passing little urine and jaundiced. Hemoglobin is 4.0 g/dL. A Giemsa-stained blood smear is shown.
oneliner: 34M + back from India + 4 d spiking fever, rigors, confusion + hypotension, oliguria, jaundice + Hb 4.0 + [blood smear] → which organism?
ask: Which organism is most likely responsible?

whyNot.A: **Months of fever**, huge spleen and low counts; amastigotes sit in macrophages, not red cells
whyNot.B: **Petechial purpuric rash** and Gram-negative diplococci; no parasites in red cells
whyNot.C: **Stepwise fever, rose spots and slow pulse**; Gram-negative rods, not red-cell parasites
whyNot.E: **Freshwater exposure and eosinophilia**; egg-shedding worm, no severe hemolysis

why: **Return from India + fever with organ failure + severe hemolytic anemia + many ring forms** = severe falciparum malaria. It invades **red cells of all ages**, giving very high parasitemia, and infected cells stick to vessel walls (PfEMP1) and block small vessels.

bug.name: Plasmodium falciparum
bug.lab: Thin smear: several rings per red cell, banana-shaped gametocytes; thick smear and rapid antigen test
bug.virulence: PfEMP1 binds endothelium (sequestration, cerebral malaria); infects red cells of all ages; no dormant liver stage
bug.spread: Female Anopheles bite; transfusion; mother to baby
bug.causes: Severe malaria: cerebral malaria, hemolytic anemia, kidney failure, ARDS

image.prompt: Giemsa-stained thin blood film: many red blood cells of normal size each with delicate small ring forms, several cells with two or three rings, some rings at the cell edge, no stippling, heavy parasitemia

stem: A 52-year-old man who had his spleen removed 5 years ago spends the summer on Long Island and has 1 week of fever, drenching sweats, dark urine and tiredness. Hemoglobin is low and bilirubin is raised. A PCR test for Plasmodium is negative. A blood smear is shown.
oneliner: 52M + splenectomy + summer on Long Island + fever, sweats, dark urine + hemolysis + Plasmodium PCR negative + [blood smear] → which organism?
ask: Which organism is most likely responsible?

whyNot.A: **Spirochete**: erythema migrans, arthritis, facial palsy; not inside red cells
whyNot.B: **Andes mountains of Peru** (sandfly); no such travel here
whyNot.C: **Unpasteurized dairy or livestock**, undulant fever; no hemolysis
whyNot.D: **Morulae in white cells** with low white count and platelets, not red-cell parasites

why: **Northeast US summer + asplenia + hemolysis + red-cell rings and Maltese cross tetrads, Plasmodium PCR negative** = Babesia microti, spread by the Ixodes (deer) tick.

bug.name: Babesia microti
bug.lab: Rings and Maltese cross tetrads in red cells; no pigment or gametocytes; PCR
bug.virulence: Infects red cells; severe in asplenia, elderly, immunosuppressed
bug.spread: Ixodes scapularis bite (can co-transmit Borrelia and Anaplasma); mouse reservoir
bug.causes: Babesiosis: fever, hemolytic anemia

image.prompt: Giemsa-stained thin blood film: red blood cells containing small pleomorphic ring forms without pigment, one cell with four merozoites arranged in a cross (Maltese cross tetrad), a few extracellular rings

stem: A 47-year-old man grew up in a mud, wood and stone house in the Brazilian Amazon and emigrated 20 years ago. He now has progressive breathlessness, orthopnea and pitting leg edema. Echocardiography shows dilation of all four chambers with poor contraction.
oneliner: 47M + childhood in mud house in Amazon + breathlessness, orthopnea, pitting edema + all four chambers dilated → which organism?
ask: Which organism most likely caused his heart disease?

whyNot.A: **Mucocutaneous ulcers** with nose and mouth destruction; not heart disease
whyNot.B: **Dysentery and liver abscess**, not cardiomyopathy
whyNot.C: **Liver fibrosis with portal hypertension**, not a dilated heart
whyNot.E: **Lymphatic filariasis**: non-pitting, thickened limb swelling and scrotal hydrocele

why: **Childhood in mud housing in Latin America + dilated biventricular failure decades later** = chronic Chagas cardiomyopathy. Reduviid bugs live in the walls; years after infection the parasite destroys heart muscle and conduction tissue.

bug.name: Trypanosoma cruzi
bug.lab: Acute: C-shaped trypomastigotes in blood; chronic: serology; amastigotes in heart muscle
bug.virulence: Invades muscle and neurons; slowly destroys heart muscle and myenteric plexus
bug.spread: Reduviid bug feces; transfusion; mother to baby
bug.causes: Acute myocarditis; chronic dilated cardiomyopathy with arrhythmias, megaesophagus, megacolon

stem: A 25-year-old man, a Marine, returns from deployment in Saudi Arabia with a painless, slowly enlarging ulcer with a raised edge on his forearm, where he was bitten by sandflies. A skin biopsy is shown.
oneliner: 25M + Marine back from Saudi Arabia + painless forearm ulcer, raised edge + sandfly bites + [skin biopsy] → which organism?
ask: Which organism is most likely responsible?

whyNot.A: **Visceral kala-azar**: fever, huge spleen and low counts, not a skin ulcer
whyNot.C: **Central and South America**, later nose and mouth destruction
whyNot.D: **Africa and tsetse fly**; parasites free in blood, not inside macrophages
whyNot.E: **Black fly bite**: itchy nodules with microfilariae, not intracellular organisms

answer: Leishmania tropica (Old World cutaneous leishmaniasis; L. major is similar)
why: **Sandfly bites in the Middle East + painless ulcer + macrophages packed with amastigotes** = Old World cutaneous leishmaniasis. The amastigotes live **inside macrophages**.

bug.name: Leishmania tropica (also L. major)
bug.type: Intracellular protozoan (amastigote in macrophages; promastigote in sandfly)
bug.lab: Amastigotes with kinetoplast in macrophages on biopsy; NNN culture
bug.virulence: Survives inside the macrophage phagolysosome
bug.spread: Phlebotomus sandfly bite
bug.causes: Old World cutaneous leishmaniasis (oriental sore)

image.prompt: Skin biopsy: macrophages packed with tiny oval intracellular organisms, each with a round nucleus and a small rod-shaped kinetoplast beside it, in a dermal inflammatory infiltrate

stem: A 31-year-old woman who emigrated from Uganda two months ago has had 2 weeks of fever and mucus-laden stools, and now has right upper abdominal tenderness. Colonoscopy shows colonic ulcers. A biopsy is shown.
oneliner: 31F + emigrated from Uganda + 2 wk fever, mucus-laden stools + RUQ tenderness + colonic ulcers + [biopsy] → which organism?
ask: Which organism is most likely responsible?

whyNot.A: **Greasy, foul diarrhea** without invasion or ulcers
whyNot.B: **Watery diarrhea** mainly in AIDS; no ulcers
whyNot.C: **Abrupt high fever and small bloody stools**; Gram-negative rod, no liver involvement
whyNot.D: **Pig exposure**; rare ciliated protozoan, no liver abscess

why: **Mucus-laden stools + undermined colonic ulcers + right upper quadrant tenderness** = amoebic colitis with spread to the liver. Trophozoites that have **eaten red cells** in a flask-shaped ulcer are the clincher.

bug.name: Entamoeba histolytica
bug.lab: Trophozoites with ingested red cells; cysts with 4 nuclei; stool antigen, serology
bug.virulence: Lectin adhesion and amoebapores lyse cells, forming flask-shaped ulcers
bug.spread: Fecal-oral; cysts in contaminated water or food
bug.causes: Dysentery, liver abscess ('anchovy paste' pus)

image.prompt: Colon biopsy: flask-shaped ulcer with undermined edges; in the ulcer base amoebic trophozoites with small eccentric nuclei and ingested red blood cells in their cytoplasm

stem: A 34-year-old man with HIV (CD4 count 30/µL) has had 10 days of watery, nonbloody diarrhea and has lost 4 kg. He has no fever, has not taken antibiotics and has not travelled. A modified acid-fast stain of his stool is shown.
oneliner: 34M + HIV, CD4 30 + 10 d watery nonbloody diarrhea + weight loss + no fever, no antibiotics, no travel + [modified acid-fast stool stain] → which organism?
ask: Which organism is most likely responsible?

whyNot.B: **Fever, night sweats and wasting**; acid-fast bacilli and positive blood cultures
whyNot.C: **Travel or contaminated water** with massive rice-water output; comma-shaped rods
whyNot.D: **Recent antibiotics**, colitis with pseudomembranes; toxin assay
whyNot.E: **Greasy, foul-smelling stools** with bloating; cysts and trophozoites on ova and parasite exam, not acid-fast

why: **AIDS + watery nonbloody diarrhea + small acid-fast oocysts in stool** = Cryptosporidium. It infects the brush border of the small intestine; diagnosis is by **modified acid-fast stain** or antigen.

bug.name: Cryptosporidium parvum
bug.lab: 4 to 6 µm oocysts, acid-fast on modified stain; stool antigen
bug.virulence: Oocysts resist chlorine; infects enterocyte brush border
bug.spread: Fecal-oral: pools, drinking water, daycare
bug.causes: Watery diarrhea, severe and prolonged in AIDS

image.prompt: Modified acid-fast stain of stool: many round oocysts about 5 micrometres across stained bright pink-red against a blue-green background, some with internal dots

stem: A 19-year-old woman has had 4 days of vulvar itching, burning on urination and a frothy yellow-green vaginal discharge. The discharge has no fishy odor and the vaginal pH is 6.0. A saline wet mount is shown.
oneliner: 19F + 4 d vulvar itching, dysuria + frothy yellow-green discharge, no fishy odor, pH 6.0 + [saline wet mount] → which organism?
ask: Which organism is most likely responsible?

whyNot.A: **Thick white cottage-cheese discharge** with normal pH; budding yeast
whyNot.B: **Thin gray discharge with fishy odor**, clue cells and little inflammation
whyNot.D: **Gram-negative diplococci** in pus; not seen moving on a wet mount
whyNot.E: **Intracellular, no motile forms**; often silent cervicitis

why: **Frothy yellow-green discharge + pH above 4.5 + motile flagellates among white cells** = trichomoniasis. It exists only as a **trophozoite** (no cyst); treat with metronidazole, and treat the partner.

bug.name: Trichomonas vaginalis
bug.lab: Wet mount: jerky motile pear-shaped flagellates; pH above 4.5; 'strawberry cervix'
bug.virulence: Adheres to genital epithelium; no cyst stage
bug.spread: Sexual contact
bug.causes: Vaginitis with frothy discharge, urethritis, preterm birth

stem: A 45-year-old woman with asthma returned 2 years ago from a long stay in Papua New Guinea. Two weeks ago she started oral prednisone for a flare. She now has abdominal pain, diarrhea, cough and an intensely itchy rash on her buttocks and thighs. Eosinophils are raised and chest x-ray shows patchy infiltrates. A photograph of the rash is shown.
oneliner: 45F + asthma, left Papua New Guinea 2 y ago + worse 2 wk after starting prednisone + abdominal pain, diarrhea, cough + itchy buttock rash [photo] + eosinophilia → which organism?
ask: Which organism is most likely responsible?

whyNot.A: **Cannot multiply in the body**, so steroids do not cause hyperinfection; mainly iron-deficiency anemia
whyNot.B: **No skin phase** and no autoinfection; large worm passed in stool
whyNot.C: **Dog and cat hookworm** (cutaneous larva migrans): slow track usually on the feet, no gut or lung disease and no flare with steroids
whyNot.E: **Freshwater exposure** and liver disease; no steroid-triggered spread

why: **Years after tropical exposure + steroids + larva currens rash + lung and gut symptoms + eosinophilia** = Strongyloides hyperinfection. Larvae **re-enter the host (autoinfection)**, so infection lasts for decades; steroids let it explode. Treat with **ivermectin** (a benzimidazole is an alternative).

bug.name: Strongyloides stercoralis
bug.lab: Rhabditiform larvae in stool; eosinophilia; serology
bug.virulence: Autoinfection through gut wall or perianal skin; hyperinfection with steroids
bug.spread: Filariform larvae in soil penetrate skin
bug.causes: Larva currens, diarrhea, pneumonitis; hyperinfection with Gram-negative sepsis in immunosuppression

image.prompt: Skin of buttock and upper thigh with a raised red urticarial linear serpiginous track several centimetres long, with scratch marks

stem: A 38-year-old man, a hunter, has had 5 days of fever, muscle pain and puffy eyelids, beginning 10 days after eating rare polar bear meat on an Arctic trip. Eosinophils and creatine kinase are raised. A biopsy of his deltoid muscle is shown.
oneliner: 38M + hunter + rare polar bear meat + fever, myalgia, puffy eyelids + eosinophilia, high CK + [muscle biopsy] → which organism?
ask: Which organism is most likely responsible?

whyNot.A: **Soil-borne eggs**; cramps and a large worm in stool, not myositis
whyNot.C: **Undercooked pork**; cysts in brain and muscle with seizures, not fever with periorbital edema
whyNot.D: **Dog roundworm** eggs from puppies; liver and eye disease, not muscle encystment
whyNot.E: **Dog tapeworm**: slow liver or lung cyst, no eosinophilic myositis

why: **Undercooked game meat + fever, myalgia, periorbital edema, eosinophilia, high CK** = trichinellosis. Larvae released in the gut invade and **encyst in skeletal muscle**, seen on biopsy as coiled larvae.

bug.name: Trichinella spiralis (Arctic game: T. nativa)
bug.lab: Eosinophilia, high CK; muscle biopsy with encysted larvae; serology
bug.virulence: Larvae invade skeletal muscle and form nurse cells
bug.spread: Eating undercooked pork or game meat (bear, walrus)
bug.causes: Fever, myalgia, periorbital edema, eosinophilia; rarely myocarditis

image.prompt: Skeletal muscle biopsy: a coiled larva inside an oval cyst within a muscle fibre, with mild chronic inflammation around it

stem: A 26-year-old man, a Peace Corps volunteer, returns from Malawi, where he swam in Lake Malawi. He has burning on urination and blood at the end of urination. Cystoscopy shows nodules in the bladder wall, ultrasound shows mild right hydronephrosis, and urine culture is sterile.
oneliner: 26M + swam in Lake Malawi + dysuria + terminal hematuria + bladder wall nodules + hydronephrosis + sterile urine culture → which organism?
ask: Which organism is most likely responsible?

whyNot.A: **Intestinal and liver disease** with portal hypertension; not bladder disease
whyNot.B: **East Asia**, with liver and spleen disease
whyNot.D: **Urine culture would be positive**; no freshwater link
whyNot.E: **Sterile pyuria** from TB, but no freshwater link; causes renal scarring and calcification

why: **Freshwater swimming in Africa + terminal hematuria + bladder nodules + hydronephrosis with sterile urine** = Schistosoma haematobium. Eggs with a **terminal spine** lodge in the bladder wall; long-term risk is **squamous cell carcinoma** of the bladder.

bug.name: Schistosoma haematobium
bug.lab: Eggs with terminal spine in urine
bug.virulence: Eggs in bladder wall cause granulomas and fibrosis; larvae penetrate skin
bug.spread: Larvae (cercariae) from freshwater snails penetrate skin
bug.causes: Hematuria, hydronephrosis, squamous cell bladder cancer; treat with praziquantel

stem: A 29-year-old man who emigrated from Central Africa has had 3 months of abdominal discomfort. He has an enlarged liver and spleen with ascites, and eosinophils are 10%. He has no urinary symptoms. A photomicrograph of his stool is shown.
oneliner: 29M + from Central Africa + 3 mo abdominal discomfort + hepatosplenomegaly, ascites + eosinophilia + no urinary symptoms + [stool photomicrograph] → which organism?
ask: Which organism is most likely responsible?

whyNot.B: **Urinary disease** with terminal-spined eggs in urine; he has no urinary symptoms
whyNot.C: **East Asia**, with a tiny knob-like spine; he is from Africa
whyNot.D: **Greasy diarrhea**; trophozoites and cysts, not eggs, and no eosinophilia
whyNot.E: **Dysentery and liver abscess**; cysts with four nuclei, not eggs

why: **Africa + hepatosplenomegaly with ascites + eosinophilia + egg with a lateral spine in stool** = Schistosoma mansoni. Eggs trapped in portal venules cause granulomas and **periportal fibrosis**, giving portal hypertension.

bug.name: Schistosoma mansoni
bug.lab: Large eggs with lateral spine in stool; eosinophilia
bug.virulence: Eggs provoke granulomas and periportal 'pipestem' fibrosis
bug.spread: Larvae (cercariae) from freshwater snails penetrate skin
bug.causes: Hepatosplenic disease, portal hypertension, varices; treat with praziquantel

image.prompt: Unstained stool wet mount: one large oval pale-yellow egg with a prominent spine projecting from its side, containing a developing larva

stem: A previously healthy 9-year-old girl whose family recently moved from rural Mexico has a first generalized seizure. She has no fever. A CT scan of her head is shown.
oneliner: 9F + previously healthy + family from rural Mexico + first generalized seizure + no fever + [head CT] → which organism?
ask: Which organism is most likely responsible?

whyNot.A: **Ring-enhancing lesions** in AIDS; she is previously healthy
whyNot.B: **Meningitis** in AIDS with fever and headache, not seizure alone
whyNot.C: **Tuberculomas and basal meningitis** with fever and cranial palsies; she has no fever
whyNot.E: **Large solitary hydatid cyst**, usually in liver or lung; brain cysts are rare

why: **Healthy child from Latin America + new seizure + multiple small cysts, some with a dot, and calcified nodules** = neurocysticercosis. It follows swallowing **T. solium eggs** (fecal-oral, from a human tapeworm carrier); larvae encyst in brain and muscle.

bug.name: Taenia solium
bug.lab: Cysticerci with scolex on CT or MRI; eggs or proglottids in stool of carrier; serology
bug.virulence: Larvae encyst in brain and muscle, then calcify
bug.spread: Eggs from human carrier (cysticercosis); undercooked pork cysts (adult tapeworm)
bug.causes: Neurocysticercosis (seizures), intestinal taeniasis; treat with albendazole or praziquantel

image.prompt: Axial CT of the head: multiple small round calcified nodules scattered through the brain, plus several small cysts each with an eccentric dot inside
